title: JavaScript
summary: The language of the browser: variables, functions, arrays, objects and async code.

lessons.title: JavaScript: syntax basics

concept.text:
JavaScript is the programming language built into every web browser. It makes pages interactive, and with Node.js it runs on servers too.

Programs store values in a variable, make decisions with `if`, and repeat work with loops. `console.log()` prints a value so you can see what your code is doing.
concept.analogy: A variable is a labelled jar. `let score = 10` puts 10 in a jar labelled score. Later you can look inside the jar, or swap what is in it.

visual.caption: The value types you will use daily.

steps.title: Declare variables
steps.text: Use `const` by default. Use `let` only when the value must change.
steps.code:
const name = 'Ava'
let score = 0
score = score + 10

steps.title: Make a decision
steps.text: Use `===` to compare. It checks value and type.

steps.title: Repeat with a loop
steps.text: `for...of` walks through each item in an array.

challenge.prompt: FizzBuzz: print the numbers 1 to 15. For multiples of 3 print `Fizz`, for multiples of 5 print `Buzz`, and for multiples of both print `FizzBuzz`.
challenge.hint: `n % 3 === 0` is true when n divides evenly by 3. Check the both case first.

takeaways: Use const by default and let when a value must change.
Compare with === and print with console.log().
Template strings with backticks insert values using ${ }.

lessons.title: JavaScript: functions, arrays, objects and async

concept.text:
A function is a reusable block of code with a name, inputs (parameters) and an output (return value). Arrays and objects hold collections of data, and array methods like `map` and `filter` transform them without manual loops.

Some work takes time, such as fetching from an API. JavaScript does not stop and wait. A slow operation returns a **promise**, and `await` pauses just that function until the result arrives.
concept.analogy: A promise is a restaurant buzzer. You order, get a buzzer straight away, and carry on chatting. When it buzzes, your food (the result) is ready.

visual.caption: Chaining array methods: each step returns a new array.

steps.title: Write a function
steps.text: Arrow functions are the short form.

steps.title: Transform arrays
steps.text: `filter` keeps items that pass a test. `map` changes every item. `find` returns the first match.
steps.code:
const users = [{ name: 'Ava', age: 30 }, { name: 'Ben', age: 17 }]
const adults = users.filter((u) => u.age >= 18).map((u) => u.name)

steps.title: Unpack objects
steps.text: Destructuring pulls fields out by name.

steps.title: Await slow things
steps.text: Mark the function `async`, then `await` promises inside it. Wrap in try/catch to handle failures.

challenge.prompt: Given the `cart` array, compute the total price of the items that are in stock. Use `filter` and `reduce`.
challenge.hint: `reduce((sum, item) => sum + item.price, 0)` adds up prices, starting from 0.
challenge.solution:
const total = cart
  .filter((c) => c.inStock)
  .reduce((sum, c) => sum + c.price, 0)
console.log(total) // 85

takeaways: Functions package logic. Arrow functions are a compact way to write them.
filter, map and reduce replace most hand-written loops.
async/await lets you write code that waits for slow work without freezing the page.

lessons.title: JavaScript mini project: a to-do list engine

concept.text: Every to-do app is the same four operations on an array of objects: add, toggle, remove and list. Build that engine as plain functions first. A user interface is just buttons that call them.
concept.analogy: The engine is the kitchen and the UI is the dining room. Get the kitchen cooking properly before you choose tablecloths.

nodes.label: new todos
nodes.detail: A fresh array, the old one untouched

steps.title: Model the data
steps.text: Each to-do is an object with an `id`, `text` and `done` flag.

steps.title: Write pure functions
steps.text: Each function takes the current list and returns a new list instead of changing the old one. This makes bugs far easier to find.
steps.code: const add = (todos, text) => [...todos, { id: Date.now(), text, done: false }]

steps.title: Render
steps.text: Turn the array into lines of text with `map` and `join`. In a browser app, you would create DOM elements here instead.

interactive.starter:
let nextId = 1
const add = (todos, text) => [...todos, { id: nextId++, text, done: false }]
const toggle = (todos, id) => todos.map((t) => (t.id === id ? { ...t, done: !t.done } : t))
const remove = (todos, id) => todos.filter((t) => t.id !== id)
const render = (todos) => todos.map((t) => `${t.done ? '[x]' : '[ ]'} ${t.id}. ${t.text}`).join('\n')

let todos = []
todos = add(todos, 'Learn JavaScript')
todos = add(todos, 'Build a project')
todos = add(todos, 'Take a break')
todos = toggle(todos, 1)
todos = remove(todos, 3)

console.log(render(todos))

challenge.prompt: Add a `stats(todos)` function that returns an object like `{ total: 2, done: 1, remaining: 1 }`, and a `clearDone(todos)` function that removes every finished item.

takeaways: App state is usually just an array of objects.
Functions that return new data instead of mutating are easier to test and debug.
Build and test the logic first, then attach a user interface.
